<!-- Generated by sourcery-ai[bot]: start review_guide -->

## Reviewer's Guide

This PR completes the cloud deployment by adding Docker and WordPress roles that provision a persistent four-service Compose stack, secure it with UFW-compatible nginx TLS routing and automated Let’s Encrypt renewal, load encrypted group secrets into a protected runtime environment, and converge WordPress configuration across repeat or multi-host deployments.

#### Sequence diagram for automated TLS bootstrap and renewal

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Ansible
    participant Nginx
    participant Certbot
    participant LetsEncrypt
    participant Systemd

    Ansible->>Nginx: Start stack with self-signed certificate
    Ansible->>Certbot: getent ahostsv4
    Ansible->>Certbot: docker compose run certonly --webroot
    Certbot->>LetsEncrypt: HTTP-01 challenge
    LetsEncrypt->>Nginx: Request challenge on port 80
    LetsEncrypt-->>Certbot: Issue certificate
    Certbot-->>Ansible: Write certificate to letsencrypt volume
    Ansible->>Nginx: nginx -s reload
    Systemd->>Certbot: certbot renew
    Certbot->>LetsEncrypt: Renew certificate when due
    Certbot->>Nginx: nginx -s reload
```

#### Flow diagram for idempotent Ansible deployment

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start[site.yml] --> Common[common role]
    Common --> Security[security role]
    Security --> Docker[Install and enable Docker Engine]
    Docker --> Secrets[Assert vault secrets are available]
    Secrets --> TLS[Generate or reuse self-signed TLS certificate]
    TLS --> Render[Render protected .env, Compose, and nginx configuration]
    Render --> Stack[Start or converge Compose stack]
    Stack --> LetsEncrypt{Let's Encrypt enabled?}
    LetsEncrypt -->|No| Install[Check and install WordPress]
    LetsEncrypt -->|Yes| DNS[Validate certificate names resolve to host]
    DNS --> Certificate[Request or reuse certificate]
    Certificate --> Reload[Reload nginx with trusted certificate]
    Reload --> Install
    Install --> URLs[Align WordPress home and siteurl]
    URLs --> Done[Repeatable multi-host deployment]
```

### File-Level Changes

| Change | Details | Files |
| ------ | ------- | ----- |
| Expand the project from baseline host provisioning into a complete containerized WordPress deployment. | <ul><li>Add a dedicated Docker role that installs Docker Engine and Compose from Docker’s repository, configures bounded JSON-file logs, enables boot startup, and optionally grants Docker-group access.</li><li>Add a WordPress role that renders the Compose stack, secret environment file, nginx configuration, and persistent stack directories.</li><li>Deploy MariaDB, WordPress PHP-FPM, phpMyAdmin PHP-FPM, and nginx with pinned images, health checks, memory limits, restart policies, named volumes, and isolated frontend/backend networks.</li><li>Ensure only nginx publishes ports while MariaDB remains on an internal network.</li></ul> | `site.yml`<br/>`requirements.yml`<br/>`roles/docker/defaults/main.yml`<br/>`roles/docker/handlers/main.yml`<br/>`roles/docker/tasks/main.yml`<br/>`roles/wordpress/defaults/main.yml`<br/>`roles/wordpress/handlers/main.yml`<br/>`roles/wordpress/tasks/main.yml`<br/>`roles/wordpress/templates/docker-compose.yml.j2`<br/>`roles/wordpress/templates/env.j2` |
| Implement automated TLS bootstrapping, certificate issuance, renewal, and name-based HTTPS routing. | <ul><li>Generate an idempotent self-signed certificate for initial nginx startup.</li><li>Preflight DNS resolution for all ACME names before requesting a certificate.</li><li>Use an ACME HTTP-01 challenge through nginx, switch vhosts to the issued certificate, and reload nginx.</li><li>Install a twice-daily systemd renewal timer and reload nginx after renewal.</li><li>Configure HTTP-to-HTTPS redirects, ACME challenge exceptions, WordPress/phpMyAdmin vhosts, and a rejecting default vhost.</li><li>Use variable-based Docker DNS upstreams so nginx tolerates PHP-FPM startup ordering.</li></ul> | `roles/wordpress/tasks/main.yml`<br/>`roles/wordpress/tasks/letsencrypt.yml`<br/>`roles/wordpress/templates/site.conf.j2`<br/>`roles/wordpress/templates/renew-cert.sh.j2`<br/>`roles/wordpress/templates/certbot-renew.service.j2`<br/>`roles/wordpress/templates/certbot-renew.timer.j2` |
| Add deployment configuration for domain-specific settings and encrypted runtime secrets. | <ul><li>Define domain, site URL, TLS, WordPress, database, and Docker-user settings in group variables.</li><li>Move live encrypted credentials to group_vars/webservers/vault.yml and validate required secrets before rendering.</li><li>Render the runtime .env with restrictive permissions and suppress secret output.</li></ul> | `group_vars/webservers/vars.yml`<br/>`group_vars/webservers/vault.yml`<br/>`roles/wordpress/tasks/main.yml`<br/>`roles/wordpress/templates/env.j2` |
| Make WordPress installation and subsequent configuration converge automatically. | <ul><li>Run first-time installation through a Compose wpcli helper container.</li><li>Synchronize stored WordPress home and site URLs on every deployment to support domain changes.</li><li>Document idempotence, multi-host inventory usage, rendered Compose location, DNS/TLS prerequisites, firewall requirements, and operational commands.</li></ul> | `roles/wordpress/tasks/main.yml`<br/>`README.md` |

<summary>Tips and commands</summary>

#### Interacting with Sourcery

- **Trigger a new review:** Comment `@sourcery-ai review` on the pull request.
- **Continue discussions:** Reply directly to Sourcery's review comments.
- **Generate a GitHub issue from a review comment:** Ask Sourcery to create an
  issue from a review comment by replying to it. You can also reply to a
  review comment with `@sourcery-ai issue` to create an issue from it.
- **Generate a pull request title:** Write `@sourcery-ai` anywhere in the pull
  request title to generate a title at any time. You can also comment
  `@sourcery-ai title` on the pull request to (re-)generate the title at any time.
- **Generate a pull request summary:** Write `@sourcery-ai summary` anywhere in
  the pull request body to generate a PR summary at any time exactly where you
  want it. You can also comment `@sourcery-ai summary` on the pull request to
  (re-)generate the summary at any time.
- **Generate reviewer's guide:** Comment `@sourcery-ai guide` on the pull
  request to (re-)generate the reviewer's guide at any time.
- **Resolve all Sourcery comments:** Comment `@sourcery-ai resolve` on the
  pull request to resolve all Sourcery comments. Useful if you've already
  addressed all the comments and don't want to see them anymore.
- **Dismiss all Sourcery reviews:** Comment `@sourcery-ai dismiss` on the pull
  request to dismiss all existing Sourcery reviews. Especially useful if you
  want to start fresh with a new review - don't forget to comment
  `@sourcery-ai review` to trigger a new review!

#### Customizing Your Experience

Access your [dashboard](https://app.sourcery.ai) to:
- Enable or disable review features such as the Sourcery-generated pull request
  summary, the reviewer's guide, and others.
- Change the review language.
- Add, remove or edit custom review instructions.
- Adjust other review settings.

#### Getting Help

- [Contact our support team](mailto:support@sourcery.ai) for questions or feedback.
- Visit our [documentation](https://docs.sourcery.ai) for detailed guides and information.
- Keep in touch with the Sourcery team by following us on [X/Twitter](https://x.com/SourceryAI), [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/sourcery-ai/) or [GitHub](https://github.com/sourcery-ai).

<details open><summary><h3>Greptile Summary</h3></summary>

The PR adds an Ansible-managed Docker deployment for WordPress, MariaDB, phpMyAdmin, nginx, and automated TLS lifecycle management. The latest changes address all three previously reported issues.
- Existing certificates are inspected for missing SANs before issuance is skipped.
- Unsupported host architectures now fail explicitly before the Docker repository architecture is selected.
- Disabling Let's Encrypt stops and removes the renewal timer, service, and script.
</details>

The PR appears safe to merge.

No blocking failure remains.
</details>


<details open><summary><h3>Important Files Changed</h3></summary>




| Filename | Overview |
|----------|----------|
| roles/wordpress/tasks/letsencrypt.yml | Inspects the existing certificate SAN list and expands the certificate when configured names are missing. |
| roles/docker/tasks/main.yml | Validates the gathered host architecture before using its explicit Docker repository mapping. |
| roles/wordpress/tasks/letsencrypt-teardown.yml | Stops and disables the renewal timer, removes renewal artifacts, and schedules a systemd daemon reload. |
| roles/wordpress/tasks/main.yml | Integrates certificate issuance and teardown into the stack deployment lifecycle. |

</details>


<details open><summary><h3>Sequence Diagram</h3></summary>

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Ansible
    participant D as Docker Compose
    participant N as nginx
    participant C as certbot
    participant S as systemd
    A->>D: Render configuration and start stack
    D->>N: Start with bootstrap certificate
    alt Let's Encrypt enabled
        A->>A: Validate DNS and certificate SANs
        A->>C: Issue or expand certificate when needed
        A->>N: Render trusted certificate paths and reload
        A->>S: Install and enable renewal timer
    else Let's Encrypt disabled
        A->>N: Render bootstrap certificate paths and reload
        A->>S: Stop timer and remove renewal units
    end
```

Hey - I've found 3 issues

<details>
<summary>Prompt for AI Agents</summary>

~~~markdown
Please address the comments from this code review:

## Individual Comments

### Comment 1
<location path="roles/wordpress/tasks/letsencrypt.yml" line_range="12-23" />
<code_context>
+# wait an hour to retry. Checking resolution ourselves turns that into an
+# instant, readable failure instead.
+- name: Resolve each certificate name from the target
+  ansible.builtin.command:
+    cmd: "getent ahostsv4 {{ item }}"
+  loop: "{{ wordpress_tls_le_domains }}"
+  register: wordpress_le_dns
+  changed_when: false
+  failed_when: false
+
+- name: Fail early when a certificate name does not point at this host
+  ansible.builtin.assert:
+    that:
+      - item.rc == 0
+      - ansible_host in item.stdout
+    fail_msg: >-
+      {{ item.item }} does not resolve to {{ ansible_host }}
</code_context>
<issue_to_address>
**issue (bug_risk):** The DNS preflight accepts a hostname when any returned IPv4 address contains `ansible_host`, while ignoring conflicting A records and all AAAA records. Let's Encrypt can therefore validate against a different address, causing issuance to fail after the preflight and potentially consuming the authorization rate limit.

**Triggers:** When a requested name has multiple addresses or an AAAA record pointing elsewhere.

**Suggested fix:** Require the complete resolved address set to match the target, or explicitly validate both A and AAAA records against the addresses that Let's Encrypt can reach.

```suggestion
  ansible.builtin.command:
    cmd: "getent ahosts {{ item }}"
  loop: "{{ wordpress_tls_le_domains }}"
  register: wordpress_le_dns
  changed_when: false
  failed_when: false

- name: Fail early when a certificate name does not point at this host
  ansible.builtin.assert:
    that:
      - item.rc == 0
      - (item.stdout_lines | map('split') | map('first') | unique | list) == [ansible_host]
```
</issue_to_address>

### Comment 2
<location path="roles/wordpress/tasks/main.yml" line_range="41-49" />
<code_context>
+# stay idempotent instead of minting a new cert (and a new browser
+# warning) every time.
+
+- name: Generate the TLS private key
+  community.crypto.openssl_privatekey:
+    path: "{{ wordpress_tls_key_path }}"
+    size: 2048
+    owner: root
+    group: root
+    mode: '0600'
+  when: wordpress_tls_self_signed
+  notify: Reload nginx
+
+- name: Generate the certificate signing request
</code_context>
<issue_to_address>
**issue (bug_risk):** Setting `wordpress_tls_self_signed: false` together with `wordpress_tls_letsencrypt: true` prevents the bootstrap certificate from being generated, but nginx is still started before certbot and is configured with a certificate path that does not exist. The stack therefore fails to bind HTTPS and certbot never gets a working HTTP service.

**Triggers:** When an operator disables self-signed generation while enabling Let's Encrypt on a fresh host.

**Suggested fix:** Reject this configuration, or always generate the bootstrap certificate whenever Let's Encrypt is enabled and no live certificate exists.
</issue_to_address>

### Comment 3
<location path="roles/wordpress/templates/site.conf.j2" line_range="33" />
<code_context>
+# Everything on :80 is redirected to TLS - except the ACME challenge,
+# which must stay on plain HTTP because that is where Let's Encrypt looks
+# to prove you control the name. Redirecting it would break renewals.
+server {
+    listen 80 default_server;
+    listen [::]:80 default_server;
+    server_name _;
+
+    location ^~ /.well-known/acme-challenge/ {
+        root /var/www/certbot;
+        default_type "text/plain";
+    }
+
+    location / {
</code_context>
<issue_to_address>
**nitpick:** Unknown HTTP hostnames are redirected to HTTPS instead of being refused with status 444, while the README and requirements checklist describe unknown vhosts as receiving 444. The same unknown request then reaches the TLS default server only if the client follows the redirect.

**Triggers:** When an HTTP request uses an unconfigured Host header and the caller expects unknown vhosts to be rejected immediately.

**Suggested fix:** Add an HTTP default-server refusal for unknown hosts while keeping the ACME challenge location available, or document that the 444 behavior applies only to HTTPS.

```suggestion
        return 444;
```
</issue_to_address>
~~~

</details>

### Sourcery assessment

**Needs a human reviewer.** 2 findings to address first, and a wrong firewall, nginx, Docker, or certificate configuration could expose the host or take the deployed site offline, and the WordPress database, uploads, credentials, and issued certificates persist in volumes or on disk after the code is reverted. The deployment is bounded to the target host and can be repaired or cleaned up, but reverting alone does not undo those persisted effects.

Blocking findings: `roles/wordpress/tasks/letsencrypt.yml:23`, `roles/wordpress/tasks/main.yml:49`
